### 01. Tesla: Controls engineering intern
May to August 2026, Giga Texas, Austin. Category: tesla.

A summer as a controls engineering intern at Giga Texas. I worked on PLC and HMI software for production equipment and on a local AI and knowledge toolkit that helps find faults faster. On the line, my electrical root-cause work started from the drawings.

- Software and controls, PLC and HMI applications: I developed and commissioned Siemens TIA Portal applications in SCL, ladder and function block diagram, on S7-1500 standard and fail-safe CPUs. That included the HMI tag models and operator workflows for production equipment.
- Software and controls, Reusable interfaces: I built reusable PLC and HMI interfaces for dock-side indication, safety reintegration acknowledge paths, process interlocks and multi-axis debounce timing. Each one was checked online with watch tables before I handed it off.
- Software and controls, Badge and RFID sign-in: I worked on badge and RFID sign-in for the production HMIs: normalizing credentials, handling the REST requests and responses, covering the SSO and tap-login paths, and fixing tags, scripts and endpoints that didn't match.
- Software and controls, Reading the old binaries: I reverse-engineered legacy authentication helper binaries into readable control flow and mapped the identity chain against the Siemens project structure. I also built a Control Center integration for this site without carrying over another plant's configuration.
- Software and controls, Interface specifications: I wrote PLC-HMI interface specifications that keep direct writes apart from cyclic abstraction layers, and put together an inventory of the plant's HMI and IPC addresses across several production lines.
- AI systems and knowledge tooling, Local model with human review: I set up a local inference workflow over a private controls corpus, for SCL and HMI authoring, fault classification and procedure routing. Nothing the model produced reached a PLC or a safety change without a person reviewing it first.
- AI systems and knowledge tooling, A second brain for controls work: The knowledge base was structured Markdown with wikilinks and frontmatter metadata. The graph rebuilt itself and linked assets, blocks, faults and procedures, so I could follow a question several links deep.
- AI systems and knowledge tooling, Skills written as contracts: I wrote the agent skills as versioned Markdown contracts. Each one listed its preconditions, inputs, steps, acceptance checks and failure modes. They covered tracing a schematic, proving out a watch table, auditing HMI tag paths and filing a post-incident report.
- AI systems and knowledge tooling, Tuned on real debug traces: I ran my own tuning loop on labeled debug traces: software faults versus power or network faults, unscanned call trees, credential parse errors. I adjusted the chunking, link density and skill wording until retrieval came back with the actual fix path.
- AI systems and knowledge tooling, Used on live incidents: On production incidents, the graph and skills pointed to the next step, from the schematic net to the diagnostics, the tag and the call tree. That cut the time to isolate repeat pendant recovery faults, intermittent dropouts and badge API faults.
- AI systems and knowledge tooling, Data stays local: No plant data went into outside training. The model and skills were only used for authoring, navigation and running runbooks.
- Electrical, schematics and root cause, Starting from the drawings: I traced power distribution, industrial network segments and safety circuits through the electrical schematics and panel drawings, and checked the hardware against the drawing package instead of guessing from the software alone.
- Electrical, schematics and root cause, Test cells: I wired and commissioned multi-device test cells with a PLC, remote I/O, an HMI, a pendant dock and a safety gate lock. On those cells I separated power and data cabling faults from application logic, and wrote up for the team how to tell them apart.
- Electrical, schematics and root cause, Intermittent faults: I led the isolation of intermittent faults on major production lines. I lined up bench baselines, PLC diagnostic buffers and the cable, switch and power paths from the schematics, and turned down raising watchdogs or timeouts as the fix.
- Electrical, schematics and root cause, Pendants that recover: I restored safety reintegration on the handheld operator pendants after a power loss, so an HMI acknowledge brings them back without a full PLC download. The causes were acknowledge tags that weren't bound and post-safety logic left out of the cyclic call tree.
- Electrical, schematics and root cause, Torque, debounce and an interlock: I fixed torque-limit selection so the at-speed limits latch after acceleration. I also put one HMI-adjustable debounce across several axes, and staged a cross-program process interlock that stays disabled until its setpoints pass safety validation.

Tools: Siemens TIA Portal, S7-1500 standard and fail-safe, SCL / LAD / FBD, HMI, Watch tables, RFID, REST, SSO, Local LLM inference, Markdown knowledge graph, Electrical schematics, Remote I/O, Industrial networks.

### 02. Music: Songwriter, producer and guitarist
Ongoing, College Station, Texas. Category: music.

I write and produce my own songs, beats and orchestral sketches, and I minor in music technology at Texas A&M. I work on engineering the same way I work on a track: get a rough version down fast, then listen hard and fix whatever doesn't feel right.

- First idea to the mix: I write, arrange and produce in Logic Pro and Ableton Live, taking a song from the first idea to the mix.
- Orchestral sketches: For orchestral sketches and mockups I use Spitfire's BBC Symphony Orchestra, which covers the strings, brass and winds.
- Guitar first: Most of my songs start on guitar. When I play parts live, I use MainStage.
- My own effects rig: I also built a DSP effects rig for my guitar. It has its own page with the engineering projects.
- Music technology: I minor in music technology at Texas A&M University.

Tools: Logic Pro, Ableton Live, MainStage, GarageBand, Spitfire BBC Symphony Orchestra, Splice, Guitar.

### 03. 4D Mapping: Object detection and AI optimization
2026, Personal project. Category: ai.

A plain 2D video goes in. Object detection finds the subject in every frame, depth models and camera solving lift each frame into 3D, and the frames join up into one scene you can orbit and scrub through time. Earlier positions stay behind as ghosts, so you see the deer's whole path through the woods at once. The demo on this page came out of my own pipeline from a single clip. No 3D scanner, no extra cameras.

- Space and time from one video: One ordinary video is enough. The pipeline solves the camera's path, tracks the subject frame by frame and places the whole scene in x, y, z and time.
- Detection, measured: On a 1,000-image hold-out set, RF-DETR large finds people at 0.878 AP@0.50 in 35 ms a frame on an M5 Max. The small model that runs on the device gets 0.489.
- What the stock detectors miss: Stock detectors miss subjects like a deer. For those, open-vocabulary detection and segmentation (Grounding DINO and SAM) find them and cut them out.
- The photoreal version: There is also a photoreal version: Gaussian splats and per-frame 3D Gaussians, trained on the real frames and scored on frames held back from training.
- Runs on its own: Drop a clip in a folder and the pipeline runs end to end and writes its own report.
- Its own app: It has its own native desktop app, written in Rust on wgpu, with a 4D timeline, orbit, top-down and follow cameras, and a way to correct detections by hand.

Tools: Python, PyTorch (Apple MPS), RF-DETR, Grounding DINO, SAM, Depth Anything 3, COLMAP, Gaussian splatting, Rust, wgpu, Core ML.

### 04. Wearable headset: Hardware startup project with a small team
2026, in development, Texas A&M, College Station. Category: headset.

A wearable I'm building with a small team at Texas A&M: a headset that watches what's coming up behind you and tells you without blocking your ears. It's early, and parts of it stay private until the team is ready, so this is the outline.

- Circuit boards: I designed custom four-layer circuit boards in KiCad, from the schematic through fabrication and assembly.
- A sensor node: I'm building a sensor node with a camera, radar and a distance sensor. Its firmware logs every reading, so tests can be replayed.
- A Mac app for the vision work: A native Mac app for the computer-vision work: live camera, object detection and a 3D replay of what the sensors saw.
- Enclosures: I designed and 3D-printed the enclosures and mounts for the prototypes.

Tools: KiCad, ESP32-S3, C++, Swift and SwiftUI, Core ML, Python, Computer vision, 3D printing.

### 05. ThinkFree Finance: Founder and software engineer
April 2025 to February 2026, College Station, Texas. Category: ai.

ThinkFree Finance explains markets for people who don't follow them for a living: renters, hourly workers, small-business owners, students. It reads the news, links it to public records and writes plain-English reports. A language model can state a wrong number as confidently as a right one, so the pipeline checks what it can and labels what it can't.

- The news pipeline: News is collected, clustered by embeddings and summarized by a language model, with FAISS retrieval over economic reference texts. It's built to handle more than 1,000 articles a day.
- Following the money: It connects politicians, bills, lobbying, congressional trades and public spending, using SEC EDGAR, OpenFEC, USASpending, BLS, Census and other public sources.
- Checking the numbers: Numbers in a generated report are checked against the source data. If a summary fails the check, it's held back.
- Website and app: A FastAPI website with accounts, MFA, CSRF protection, role-based access and a hash-chained audit log, plus a SwiftUI iPhone app.
- My own security review: In October 2026 I did my own security review. Every bug I found is logged with the test that proves it's fixed.

Tools: Python, FastAPI, FAISS, Sentence embeddings, LLM APIs, JavaScript, SwiftUI, pytest.
Link: [github / thinkfreefinance](https://github.com/allanaziz581/ThinkFreeFinance)

### 06. hardcaml-pwm: Digital hardware design in OCaml
October 2026. Category: engineering.

A small piece of digital hardware, written in OCaml with Jane Street's Hardcaml. Turn a rotary encoder and the PWM output follows, sliding to the new duty cycle over a few periods instead of jumping there. It's simulated and tested, and the Verilog is generated. It's still a learning project, though, and hasn't run on an FPGA board yet.

- A PWM that glides: Each new duty-cycle target ramps in over a fixed number of periods and lands exactly, with no rounding error.
- Reading the encoder: A quadrature decoder for an EC11-style rotary encoder: synchronizers, debouncing, direction from the A and B edges, and a click only on a real detent.
- Tested in simulation: Every block has waveform tests in simulation, and the Verilog comes straight out of the OCaml.

Tools: OCaml, Hardcaml, Verilog, Simulation, Expect tests.
Link: [github / hardcaml-pwm](https://github.com/allanaziz581/hardcaml-pwm)

### 07. DSP guitar rig: Effects hardware for guitar

A digital signal-processing effects system for my own guitar, so it's engineering and music in one project. It started on a breadboard, and I tested it there.

- On a breadboard: I breadboarded the signal chain, from the guitar input to the processed output.
- Tested by ear: I tested it on the bench and by ear.

Tools: DSP, Breadboard prototyping, Guitar.

Link: [github / the-brute-vr](https://github.com/aggie-coding-club/the-brute-vr)
